questionText: 25 trays: cup only or plate only or both. 15 have cups, 21 have plates. Both?
hints: Some trays are counted twice, once for the cup and once for the plate. Think about what happens when you add the two groups.
Add the trays with cups and the trays with plates. Then compare that total with the real number of trays.
Here is a similar one: 30 children each like mango, banana or both. 18 like mango and 20 like banana. 18 + 20 = 38. That is 8 more than 30, so 8 children like both.

stepByStep.text: Add the trays with cups and the trays with plates.
There are only 25 trays. The extra ones were counted twice, because they have both a cup and a plate.
So 11 trays have both a cup and a plate.

misconceptions.A: This is 25 − 21, the trays with no plate. Add 15 and 21 first, then see how much more than 25 that is.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 15 + 21 = 36, which is 11 more than 25. So 11 trays were counted twice.
misconceptions.C: This is every tray with a cup. Some of those have only a cup. Add both groups and compare with 25.
misconceptions.D: This is 21 − 15. Instead, add 15 and 21 and then take away 25.

questionText: Teacher's 3-digit odd number: hundreds digit >8, tens digit 4 more than ones, sum of digits?
hints: This is a digit clue puzzle. Use one clue at a time to pin down each digit.
Start with the hundreds digit. Which single digit is more than 8?

Here is a similar one: a 3-digit number has a hundreds digit more than 8, a ones digit of 4, and a tens digit that is 2 more than the ones digit. The digits are 9, 6 and 4, so the number is 964. Sum of digits: 9 + 6 + 4 = 19.

stepByStep.text: The only digit more than 8 is 9. So the hundreds digit is 9.
The number is odd, so the ones digit is odd. The tens digit is 4 more and must still be a single digit. So the ones digit can only be 1, 3 or 5.
Try ones digit 1. Then the tens digit is 5 and the number is 951.
Add the digits of 951.
The other two numbers, 973 and 995, give 19 and 23, which are not among the choices. So the sum of the digits is 15.

misconceptions.A: With 9 in the hundreds place, the other two digits would add up to only 2. Then the tens digit could not be 4 more than the ones digit.
misconceptions.B: With 9 in the hundreds place, the other two digits would be 4 and 0. A number ending in 0 is even, but this number is odd.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The number 951 fits every clue, and 9 + 5 + 1 = 15.
misconceptions.D: With 9 in the hundreds place, the other two digits would be 6 and 2. A number ending in 2 is even, but this number is odd.

questionText: 5-digit number 213ab, remainder <10 when ÷100. Sum of all digits = 13. Find b.
hints: This puzzle gives two clues about the digits. One is about dividing by 100 and the other is about adding the digits.
When you divide by 100, the remainder is made of the last two digits. If that remainder is less than 10, what must the tens digit a be?
Here is a similar one: 521ab leaves a remainder less than 10 when divided by 100, and its digits add up to 11. So a = 0. Then 5 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 8, and b = 11 − 8 = 3.

stepByStep.text: When you divide by 100, the remainder is the last two digits, ab.
The remainder is less than 10, so the tens digit a must be 0.
Add the digits you know.
All five digits add up to 13, so b is what is left.
So b = 7.

misconceptions.A: With b = 5 the digits add up to 2 + 1 + 3 + 0 + 5 = 11, not 13. Find what must be added to 6 to make 13.
misconceptions.B: With b = 6 the digits add up to 2 + 1 + 3 + 0 + 6 = 12, not 13. Find what must be added to 6 to make 13.
misconceptions.D: With b = 8 the digits add up to 2 + 1 + 3 + 0 + 8 = 14, not 13. Find what must be added to 6 to make 13.

questionText: Product of (□□7) and (□□8), □ not same?
hints: Some digits are hidden, so you cannot work out one exact product. Look for clues that every such product must obey.
Multiply the two ones digits you can see, 7 and 8. The product must end in the same digit as that.
Here is a similar one: (□3) × (□4), two 2-digit numbers. 3 × 4 = 12, so the product ends in 2. The smallest it can be is 13 × 14 = 182 and the largest is 93 × 94 = 8742.

stepByStep.text: Look at the ones digits. The product must end in 6.
Both numbers have 3 digits. The smallest product is 107 × 108.
The largest product is 997 × 998.
10552 and 9786 are too small. 9950006 is too big.
Only 308256 ends in 6 and is the right size. For example, 507 × 608 = 308256. So the product can be 308256.

misconceptions.A: 7 × 8 = 56, so the product must end in 6. This one ends in 2, and it is also smaller than 107 × 108.
misconceptions.B: It ends in 6, but it is too small. Even 107 × 108 is 11556.
misconceptions.C: Yes! It ends in 6 and it sits between the smallest and the largest possible products.
misconceptions.D: It ends in 6, but it is too big. Even 997 × 998 is only 995006.

questionText: Magic square: 4,5,7/2,2,2/64,100,A. Find A?
hints: Look for one rule that links the numbers going down each column. The same rule must work in every column.
Look at the first column: 4, 2 and 64. Multiply the top two numbers, and see how the result is linked to 64.
Here is a similar one: a column holds 3, 2 and 36. 3 × 2 = 6 and 6 × 6 = 36. With the same rule, a column that starts 6, 2 ends in 12 × 12 = 144.

stepByStep.text: First column: 4 × 2 = 8, and 8 × 8 = 64.
Second column: 5 × 2 = 10, and 10 × 10 = 100. The rule works again.
Third column: multiply the top two numbers.
Now multiply 14 by itself. So A = 196.

misconceptions.A: 169 is 13 × 13. The rule needs 7 × 2 first, and that is 14.
misconceptions.B: 225 is 15 × 15. Check 7 × 2 once more. It is 14.
misconceptions.C: 81 is 9 × 9, which comes from adding 7 and 2. The rule multiplies the top two numbers.

questionText: 2-digit × 3-digit: (*8)×(**7). Which can be product?
hints: Some digits are hidden, so you cannot work out one exact product. Look for clues that every such product must obey.
Multiply the two ones digits you can see, 8 and 7. The product must end in the same digit as that.
Here is a similar one: (□2) × (□□3), a 2-digit number times a 3-digit number. 2 × 3 = 6, so the product ends in 6. The smallest it can be is 12 × 103 = 1236 and the largest is 92 × 993 = 91356.

stepByStep.text: Look at the ones digits. The product must end in 6.
The smallest product is 18 × 107.
The largest product is 98 × 997.
977006 is too big and 1506 is too small. 97704 ends in 4, not 6.
Only 97706 fits. It is the largest product, 98 × 997. So the product can be 97706.

misconceptions.A: It ends in 6, but it has too many digits. The largest possible product is 98 × 997.
misconceptions.B: Yes! It ends in 6, and 98 × 997 gives exactly this number.
misconceptions.C: It ends in 6, but it is too small. The smallest possible product is 18 × 107 = 1926.
misconceptions.D: 8 × 7 = 56, so the product must end in 6. This one ends in 4.

questionText: Look at this square of numbers. Top row: 7, 13, 24. Middle row: 3, 6, Z. Bottom row: 16, 49, 169. The numbers going down each column follow the same rule. Which number is in place of Z?
hints: Read each column from top to bottom. See how the top two numbers can be used to make the bottom number.
Look at the first column: 7, 3, 16. Find 7 − 3, then think how that answer is linked to 16. Check the idea on the second column.
Similar example: a column reads 9, 4, 25. 9 − 4 = 5 and 5 × 5 = 25. If another column reads 15, ?, 64, then 8 × 8 = 64, so the difference is 8 and the missing number is 15 − 8 = 7.

stepByStep.text: First column: subtract the middle number from the top number, then multiply the answer by itself.
The second column follows the same rule.
Third column: the bottom number is 169, and 13 times 13 is 169. So 24 minus Z must be 13.
So Z is 11.

misconceptions.A: 13 is the difference that gives 169, because 13 × 13 = 169. Z is the number you take from 24 to leave 13.
misconceptions.B: 24 − 15 = 9, and 9 × 9 = 81, not 169. The difference needs to be 13.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 24 − 11 = 13 and 13 × 13 = 169, just like the other two columns.
misconceptions.D: 24 − 8 = 16, and 16 × 16 = 256, not 169. The difference needs to be 13.

questionText: Which of the following can be the product of (★ ★ 6) and (★ 9), where ★ denotes digits not necessarily the same?
hints: You cannot know the hidden digits, but you can still check two things about the product: its last digit and its size.
Multiply the last digits, 6 × 9, to find what the product must end in. Then think how small and how big a 3-digit number times a 2-digit number can be.

Similar example: (★ ★ 3) × (★ 7). 3 × 7 = 21, so the product ends in 1. The smallest it can be is 103 × 17 = 1751 and the largest is 993 × 97 = 96321. So 1231 is too small, but 10011 fits, because 213 × 47 = 10011.

stepByStep.text: Multiply the last digits to find the last digit of the product. It must end in 4.
All four choices end in 4, so check the size next. The smallest possible product is 106 times 19.
The largest possible product is 996 times 99. So 1854 is too small and 986004 is too big.
For 40548, a 2-digit number ending in 9 would have to divide it exactly. None of 19, 29, 39, 49, 59, 69, 79, 89 or 99 does.
For the choice that is left, 876 times 59 fits the pattern. So the product can be 51684.

misconceptions.A: This is too small. Even the smallest numbers that fit, 106 and 19, give 2014.
misconceptions.B: This is too big. Even the largest numbers that fit, 996 and 99, give only 98604, which has five digits.
misconceptions.C: Yes! It ends in 4, it is the right size, and 876 × 59 = 51684 fits the pattern.
misconceptions.D: The last digit and the size both look fine, so this was a careful try. But no 2-digit number ending in 9 divides 40548 exactly, so it cannot be made.

questionText: Look at this square of numbers. Top row: 3, 7, 8. Middle row: 9, 21, 24. Bottom row: 81, 441, Q. The numbers going down each column follow the same rule. Find Q.
hints: Read each column from top to bottom. Find how the top number becomes the middle number, and how the middle number becomes the bottom number.
Look at the first column: 3, 9, 81. What do you do to 3 to get 9? What do you do to 9 to get 81? Check that the second column works the same way.
Similar example: a column reads 2, 6, 36. The top number is multiplied by 3 to get 6, and 6 is multiplied by itself to get 36. A column starting with 5 would then read 5, 15, 225.

stepByStep.text: First column: 3 becomes 9, then 9 becomes 81.
The second column follows the same rule: multiply by 3, then multiply the result by itself.
Third column: 8 times 3 is 24, so Q is 24 times 24.
So Q is 576.

misconceptions.A: 196 is 14 × 14. The number above Q is 24, so Q should be 24 multiplied by itself.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Each bottom number is the middle number times itself, and 24 × 24 = 576.
misconceptions.C: 484 is 22 × 22. The number above Q is 24, so work out 24 × 24.
misconceptions.D: 676 is 26 × 26. The number above Q is 24, so Q is 24 × 24.

questionText: Magic square: n,_,6/4,x,m/16,_,_. Find (m+n).
hints: In a magic square every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total. Look for two lines that share a square.
The middle row 4, x, m and the diagonal 6, x, 16 both pass through x. So the other two numbers in each line must add up to the same amount.
Here is a similar one: in a magic square the middle row is 3, x, m and a diagonal is 5, x, 9. Both lines hold x, so 3 + m = 5 + 9 = 14. That gives m = 14 − 3 = 11.

stepByStep.text: The middle row 4, x, m and the diagonal 6, x, 16 share x. So 4 + m must equal 6 + 16.
Find m.
In a 3 by 3 magic square, each line adds up to 3 times the middle number. The diagonal is 22 + x, so 22 is 2 times x. That makes x = 11 and each line adds up to 33.
The first column is n, 4 and 16. Find n.
Add m and n. So m + n = 31.

misconceptions.A: Yes! m = 18 and n = 13, so m + n = 31.
misconceptions.B: 22 is 6 + 16, the two ends of the diagonal. Use it to find m, then find n as well.
misconceptions.C: Check n once more. The first column n + 4 + 16 must add up to the magic total, 33.
misconceptions.D: Check both parts. m comes from 4 + m = 22, and n comes from n + 4 + 16 = 33.

questionText: Product of ★★8 and ★6, where ★ not same?
hints: Some digits are hidden, so you cannot work out one exact product. Look for clues that every such product must obey.
Multiply the two ones digits you can see, 8 and 6. The product must end in the same digit as that.
Here is a similar one: (□□3) × (□4), a 3-digit number times a 2-digit number. 3 × 4 = 12, so the product ends in 2. The smallest it can be is 103 × 14 = 1442 and the largest is 993 × 94 = 93342.

stepByStep.text: Look at the ones digits. The product must end in 8.
The smallest product is 108 × 16. So 1658 is too small.
The largest product is 998 × 96. So 980808 is too big.
87604 ends in 4, not 8.
Only 43928 fits. For example, 578 × 76 = 43928. So the product can be 43928.

misconceptions.A: It ends in 8, but it is too small. Even 108 × 16 is 1728.
misconceptions.B: It ends in 8, but it has too many digits. Even 998 × 96 is only 95808.
misconceptions.C: 8 × 6 = 48, so the product must end in 8. This one ends in 4.
misconceptions.D: Yes! It ends in 8 and it is the right size for a 3-digit number times a 2-digit number.

questionText: Queue of 63 students. You are 13th from beginning, friend is 19th from end. Students between you?
hints: The two places are counted from different ends of the queue. Count both from the same end before you compare them.
Find your friend's place from the beginning. There are 18 students standing behind your friend.

Here is a similar one: 50 students in a queue. You are 10th from the beginning and your friend is 12th from the end. 11 students are behind your friend, so your friend is 50 − 11 = 39th. Between you: 39 − 10 − 1 = 28 students.

stepByStep.text: Your friend is 19th from the end, so 18 students stand behind your friend. Find your friend's place from the beginning.
You are 13th and your friend is 45th. The students between you stand in places 14 to 44.
Count them. So 31 students are between you.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Your friend is 45th from the beginning, and places 14 to 44 hold 31 students.
misconceptions.B: Check your friend's place from the beginning first. It is 45th. Then count the places from 14 to 44.
misconceptions.C: This is 45 − 13. That count includes your friend. Take away 1 more.
misconceptions.D: This comes from putting your friend in place 44. With 18 students behind, your friend is 45th.

questionText: Product of (**4) and (**8), * not same?
hints: Some digits are hidden, so you cannot work out one exact product. Look for clues that every such product must obey.
Multiply the two ones digits you can see, 4 and 8. The product must end in the same digit as that.
Here is a similar one: (□□3) × (□□5), two 3-digit numbers. 3 × 5 = 15, so the product ends in 5. The smallest it can be is 103 × 105 = 10815 and the largest is 993 × 995 = 988035.

stepByStep.text: Look at the ones digits. The product must end in 2.
Both numbers have 3 digits. The smallest product is 104 × 108. So 10992 is too small.
The largest product is 994 × 998. So 9092012 is too big.
564976 ends in 6, not 2.
Only 672672 fits. For example, 784 × 858 = 672672. So the product can be 672672.

misconceptions.A: Yes! It ends in 2 and it sits between the smallest and the largest possible products.
misconceptions.B: 4 × 8 = 32, so the product must end in 2. This one ends in 6.
misconceptions.C: It ends in 2, but it has too many digits. Even 994 × 998 is only 992012.
misconceptions.D: It ends in 2, but it is too small. Even 104 × 108 is 11232.

questionText: A 3 by 3 magic square has top row 4, 3, 8 and middle row 9, 5, 1. The bottom row is still empty. When the magic square is completed, which of these numbers will not be used?
hints: In a magic square every row and every column adds up to the same total. Find the total from a full row, then fill in the empty row.
Add the top row: 4 + 3 + 8. Each column must reach the same total, so work out what is missing under 4 and 9, under 3 and 5, and under 8 and 1.

Similar example: a magic square has top row 2, 7, 6 and middle row 9, 5, 1. Each line adds up to 15. The first column has 2 + 9, so it needs 4. The second has 7 + 5, so it needs 3. The third has 6 + 1, so it needs 8. The bottom row is 4, 3, 8.

stepByStep.text: Find the total of a full row.
Each column must also add up to 15. The first column already has 4 and 9.
Do the same for the second and third columns.
The bottom row is 2, 7, 6. The finished square uses the numbers 1 to 9, once each.
3, 6 and 9 are all in the square. The number that will not be used is 11.

misconceptions.A: 3 is already in the top row, so it is used. Look for a number that is not in the finished square.
misconceptions.B: 6 goes in the bottom row, under 8 and 1, because 8 + 1 + 6 = 15. So it is used.
misconceptions.C: 9 is already in the middle row, so it is used. The finished square holds the numbers 1 to 9.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The finished square uses 1 to 9 once each, so 11 never appears.

questionText:
In this magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total.
Row 1: 9, 2, 7
Row 2: 4, 6, 8
Row 3: 5, ?, 3
Which number is missing?
hints: In a magic square every line has the same total. Find that total from a line with no number missing.

A similar problem: a magic square has rows 8, 1, 6 and 3, 5, 7 and 4, ?, 2. Row 1 adds to 15. Row 3 has 4 + 2 = 6, so the missing number is 15 − 6 = 9.

stepByStep.text: Find the magic total from Row 1.
Row 3 must also add up to 18.
The missing number is 10.

misconceptions.A: With 9, Row 3 would add up to 17, one short of the magic total of 18.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 5 + 10 + 3 = 18, the same as every other line.
misconceptions.C: With 11, Row 3 would add up to 19, one more than the magic total of 18.

questionText: I am a 2-digit number. My tens digit is 4. My two digits add up to 11. Which number am I?
hints: Use one clue at a time. The first clue fixes one digit, and the second clue gives the other.
The tens digit is 4. What must the ones digit be so that the two digits add up to 11?
A similar problem: a 2-digit number has tens digit 3 and its digits add up to 8. The ones digit is 8 − 3 = 5, so the number is 35.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit is 4.
Find the ones digit.
The number is 47.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The tens digit is 4 and 4 + 7 = 11.
misconceptions.B: The digits do add up to 11, but here 4 is the ones digit. The clue says 4 is the tens digit.
misconceptions.C: This joins the tens digit 4 with the first digit of 11. The ones digit should be 11 − 4.
misconceptions.D: These digits add up to 11, but the tens digit is 5. The clue says the tens digit is 4.

questionText: In the sum 4P + 25 = 71, the letter P stands for one digit, so 4P is a two-digit number. Which digit is P?
hints: A missing number in an addition can be found by working backwards with subtraction.
Find the number that must be added to 25 to make 71. Its ones digit is P.
A similar problem: in 3R + 14 = 52, the first number is 52 − 14 = 38. So 3R is 38 and R is 8.

stepByStep.text: Work backwards to find the two-digit number 4P.
So 4P is 46.
P is 6.

misconceptions.A: This is the tens digit of 46. The letter P is in the ones place.
misconceptions.B: This is the ones digit of 25. Subtract 25 from 71 to find the number 4P.
misconceptions.C: You got it! 46 + 25 = 71, so P is 6.
misconceptions.D: Try it: 47 + 25 = 72, which is one too many. Subtract 25 from 71 to find 4P.

questionText: In a picture puzzle, a star plus a star makes 14. A star plus a moon makes 10. What is the moon worth?
hints: Start with the clue that has only one kind of shape. Once you know that shape, use it in the other clue.
Two stars make 14. Find what one star is worth.
A similar problem: a sun plus a sun makes 12, so a sun is 6. A sun plus a cloud makes 8, so the cloud is 8 − 6 = 2.

stepByStep.text: Two equal stars make 14, so find one star.
A star plus a moon makes 10.
The moon is worth 3.

misconceptions.A: This is what the star is worth. Use it in the second clue to find the moon.
misconceptions.B: This is 14 − 10. First halve 14 to find the star, then take the star away from 10.
misconceptions.C: This halves 10, as if the star and the moon were equal. The star is worth 7, so the moon is 10 − 7.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! The star is 7, and 7 + 3 = 10.

questionText: Amit is taller than Bina. Bina is taller than Chetan. Divya is shorter than Chetan. Who is the tallest of the four?
hints: Put the children in order of height, using one clue at a time.
Write the names in a line from tallest to shortest. Start with Amit and Bina, then fit Chetan in.
A similar problem: Ria is taller than Sam, and Sam is taller than Tia. From tallest to shortest the order is Ria, Sam, Tia, so Ria is the tallest.

stepByStep.text: Amit is taller than Bina, and Bina is taller than Chetan. So the order is Amit, Bina, Chetan.
Divya is shorter than Chetan, so she comes last: Amit, Bina, Chetan, Divya.
The tallest is Amit.

misconceptions.A: Bina is taller than Chetan, but the first clue says Amit is taller than Bina.
misconceptions.B: Chetan is taller than Divya only. Bina and Amit are both taller than Chetan.
misconceptions.C: Well done! From tallest to shortest the order is Amit, Bina, Chetan, Divya.
misconceptions.D: Divya is shorter than Chetan, so she is the shortest of the four.

questionText: In a magic square, every row adds up to 21. One row has the numbers 4 and 11 and one missing number. What is the missing number?
hints: The three numbers in the row must add up to the magic total. Two of them are known.
Add 4 and 11. Then find how much more is needed to reach 21.
A similar problem: a row must add up to 15 and has 2 and 9. Those make 11, so the missing number is 15 − 11 = 4.

stepByStep.text: Add the two numbers you know.
Find what is needed to reach 21.
The missing number is 6.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 4 + 11 + 6 = 21.
misconceptions.B: With 7 the row would add up to 22. Check the subtraction 21 − 15.
misconceptions.C: This is 4 + 11, the total of the two known numbers. Take it away from 21 to find the missing one.
misconceptions.D: This adds all three numbers, 4 + 11 + 21. The 21 is the total of the row, so subtract instead.

questionText: Two signs are missing: 8 __ 4 __ 2 = 10. Which two signs, in this order, make it true?
hints: Try each pair of signs in turn and work out the answer it gives.
The answer 10 is a little more than 8. Think about which first sign makes 8 bigger, and what the second sign must then do.
A similar problem: for 9 __ 3 __ 2 = 8, the answer is a little less than 9, so try minus first: 9 − 3 = 6. Then 6 must become 8, so add 2. The signs there are minus, then plus.

stepByStep.text: Try plus first.
Now 12 must become 10, so subtract 2.
The signs are plus, then minus.

misconceptions.A: This gives 8 − 4 + 2 = 6, which is less than 10.
misconceptions.B: This gives 8 + 4 + 2 = 14, which is more than 10.
misconceptions.C: This gives 8 × 4 − 2 = 30, which is far more than 10.
misconceptions.D: You got it! 8 + 4 − 2 = 10.

questionText: A palindrome number reads the same forwards and backwards, like 353. Which of these is a palindrome number?
hints: Read each number from right to left and compare it with the number read from left to right.
In a 4-digit palindrome, the first digit matches the last digit and the second digit matches the third. Check each number for this.
A similar problem: 4004 read backwards is 4004, so it is a palindrome. 4040 read backwards is 0404, so it is not.

stepByStep.text: Write each number backwards: 1212 becomes 2121, 1122 becomes 2211, and 2121 becomes 1212. These all change.
1221 written backwards is still 1221.
The palindrome number is 1221.

misconceptions.C: Read backwards, this becomes 2211, which is a different number.
misconceptions.D: Read backwards, this becomes 1212, which is a different number.

questionText: In the sum 3P + P8 = 82, the letter P stands for the same digit both times. 3P and P8 are two-digit numbers. Which digit is P?
hints: Look at the ones column first. The ones digits must add up to a number that ends in the ones digit of the answer.
In the ones column, P + 8 must end in 2. Which digit added to 8 gives a number ending in 2?
A similar problem: in 1R + R6 = 49, the ones column says R + 6 must end in 9, so R is 3. Check the whole sum: 13 + 36 = 49. It is true, so R is 3.

stepByStep.text: In the ones column, P + 8 must end in 2. Since 4 + 8 = 12, P could be 4.
Check the whole sum with P as 4.
The sum is true, so P is 4.

misconceptions.A: Great thinking! 34 + 48 = 82.
misconceptions.B: Try it: 35 + 58 = 93, which is more than 82. Look at the ones column: P + 8 must end in 2.
misconceptions.C: Try it: 33 + 38 = 71, which is less than 82. Look at the ones column: P + 8 must end in 2.
misconceptions.D: This is 8 − 2 from the ones column. The ones digits are added, so P + 8 must end in 2.

questionText: P and Q are digits. The two-digit numbers PQ and QP add up to 77, and P is 1 more than Q. What is the number PQ?
hints: When a two-digit number is added to its reverse, each column adds the same two digits. Find what the two digits add up to.
In the ones column, Q + P must give 7. Now find two digits that add up to 7 where one is 1 more than the other.

questionText: I think of a number. I double it and then add 3. The answer is 17. What number did I think of?
hints: Work backwards from the answer, undoing each step in the opposite order.
The last thing done was adding 3. Undo that first by taking 3 away from 17.
A similar problem: I double a number and add 5 to get 25. Undo the adding: 25 − 5 = 20. Undo the doubling: 20 ÷ 2 = 10. The number was 10.

stepByStep.text: Undo the adding of 3.
Undo the doubling.
Check.
The number was 7.

misconceptions.A: This adds 3 to 17 and then halves. To undo adding 3, take 3 away.
misconceptions.B: This undoes the adding but stops there. The doubling must be undone too, by halving 14.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 7 doubled is 14, and 14 + 3 = 17.
misconceptions.D: This doubles 17 and adds 3. That repeats the steps instead of undoing them.

questionText: Isha, Jay, Kiran and Lata each have one pet: a cat, a dog, a parrot and a rabbit. Jay has the cat. Kiran has the rabbit. Isha does not have the dog. Which pet does Lata have?
hints: Cross off the pets that are already taken, then use the last clue to decide between the pets that are left.

A similar problem: Om, Pia and Raj have a ball, a kite and a top. Om has the ball. Pia does not have the kite. So Pia has the top, and Raj has the kite.

stepByStep.text: Jay has the cat and Kiran has the rabbit, so the dog and the parrot are left for Isha and Lata.
Isha does not have the dog, so Isha has the parrot.
The only pet left for Lata is the dog.

misconceptions.A: The parrot belongs to Isha, because Isha does not have the dog and the other pets are taken.
misconceptions.B: The first clue says that Jay has the cat.
misconceptions.C: The second clue says that Kiran has the rabbit.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! The dog and the parrot were left, Isha took the parrot, so Lata has the dog.

questionText: I am a 2-digit number less than 50. I am a multiple of 7. My digits add up to 6. Which number am I?
hints: Use the clue that leaves the fewest numbers first, list them, then test each with the other clue.
List the 2-digit multiples of 7 that are less than 50. Then add the digits of each one.
A similar problem: a 2-digit multiple of 9 less than 40 whose digits differ by 5. The multiples are 18, 27 and 36. Only 27 has digits that differ by 5, so the number is 27.

stepByStep.text: The 2-digit multiples of 7 below 50 are 14, 21, 28, 35, 42 and 49.
Their digit totals are 5, 3, 10, 8, 6 and 13.
Only one has digits adding up to 6. The number is 42.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 42 = 7 × 6, and 4 + 2 = 6.
misconceptions.B: The digits add up to 6, but 24 is not a multiple of 7. Try the same digits the other way round.
misconceptions.C: 35 is a multiple of 7, but its digits add up to 8.
misconceptions.D: The digits add up to 6, but 33 is not in the table of 7.

questionText: A pencil and an eraser together cost ₹12. Two pencils and an eraser together cost ₹19. How much does the eraser cost?
hints: Compare the two purchases. Look at what the second one has that the first one does not.

stepByStep.text: The second purchase has one extra pencil. Find its cost.

The eraser costs ₹5.

misconceptions.B: Well done! The pencil costs ₹7, so the eraser costs 12 − 7 = ₹5.
misconceptions.C: This halves ₹12, as if the pencil and the eraser cost the same. The extra pencil in the second purchase shows a pencil costs ₹7.
misconceptions.D: The pencil costs ₹7. Check the subtraction 12 − 7 once more.

misconceptions.C: Excellent! 245 × 3 = 735, so R is 4.

questionText: Five children ran a race. Dev finished after Farah but before Esha. Hari finished between Dev and Esha. Gita finished last. Who came second?
hints: Draw five blanks for the five places and fit the children in, one clue at a time.

questionText: A two-digit number ending in 3 is multiplied by a two-digit number ending in 4. Which of these can be the product?
hints: You cannot find the exact numbers, so test each choice instead. Check its last digit, and check whether its size is possible.
The last digit of the product comes from 3 × 4. Which choices end in the right digit? Then think about the smallest and largest products possible.

A similar problem: a two-digit number ending in 2 times a two-digit number ending in 6 must end in 2, because 2 × 6 = 12. The smallest such product is 12 × 16 = 192 and the largest is 92 × 96 = 8832. So 1472 is possible (it is 32 × 46), but 9992 is too big.

stepByStep.text: Find the last digit of the product.
So the product ends in 2. This rules out 1037.
Find the smallest and largest possible products.
172 is smaller than 182 and 9872 is bigger than 8742, so neither is possible.
The one left is possible.
The product can be 1032.

misconceptions.A: This ends in 7, which comes from adding 3 and 4. In a product the last digit comes from 3 × 4 = 12, so it must be 2.
misconceptions.B: This ends in 2, but it is too big. The largest possible product is 93 × 94 = 8742.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! It ends in 2 and lies between 182 and 8742. In fact 43 × 24 = 1032.
misconceptions.D: This ends in 2, but it is too small. The smallest possible product is 13 × 14 = 182.

questionText: In the sum P + P + P = QP, the letters P and Q stand for two different digits, and QP is a two-digit number. What is P + Q?
hints: Look at the ones digit. Three times the digit P gives a number that ends in P again. Very few digits can do that.
Test the digits one by one: 3 × 1 = 3, 3 × 2 = 6, and so on. Look for a two-digit answer whose ones digit is the digit you started with.
A similar problem: R + R + R + R + R + R = 2R, where 2R is a two-digit number that starts with 2. Six times R must end in R and lie in the twenties. Since 6 × 4 = 24, R is 4.

stepByStep.text: Three times P must end in the digit P and must be a two-digit number.
Testing the digits, only 5 works.
So P is 5 and QP is 15, which makes Q equal to 1.
Add the two digits.

misconceptions.A: This is P alone. The sum 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 shows that Q is 1, so add it on.
misconceptions.B: This is the two-digit number QP. The question asks for the digits P and Q added together.
misconceptions.C: P is 5, and 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so Q is 1 and not 2.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so P is 5, Q is 1, and 5 + 1 = 6.

questionText: I am a 3-digit number. My hundreds digit is double my ones digit. My tens digit equals my hundreds digit plus my ones digit. My three digits add up to 12. Which number am I?
hints: Every digit can be described using the ones digit. Try small values for the ones digit and see which one fits all the clues.
If the ones digit is 1, the hundreds digit is 2 and the tens digit is 2 + 1 = 3. Do these digits add up to 12? If not, try ones digit 2.

A similar problem: the hundreds digit is three times the ones digit, the tens digit is their total, and the digits add up to 8. With ones digit 1, the hundreds digit is 3 and the tens digit is 4. Since 3 + 4 + 1 = 8, the number is 341.

stepByStep.text: Try ones digit 1: hundreds digit 2, tens digit 3. The digits add up to 6, which is too small.
Try ones digit 2: hundreds digit 4, tens digit 6.
All the clues fit.
The number is 462.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 4 is double 2, 6 = 4 + 2, and 4 + 6 + 2 = 12.
misconceptions.B: These are the right digits in reverse order. The hundreds digit must be double the ones digit, so 4 goes in the hundreds place.
misconceptions.C: Here the hundreds digit 6 is three times the ones digit 2. It should be double, and the tens digit should be the total of the other two.
misconceptions.D: This fits the first two clues, but its digits add up to only 6. They must add up to 12.

questionText: A farmer has hens and goats. Together they have 10 heads and 28 legs. How many goats does the farmer have?
hints: Each animal has one head, so you know how many animals there are. Suppose they were all hens and see how many legs are missing.
There are 10 animals. If all 10 were hens, how many legs would there be? Compare that with 28.
A similar problem: 5 heads and 14 legs. If all 5 were hens there would be 10 legs. The 4 extra legs come from goats, which have 2 more legs each, so there are 4 ÷ 2 = 2 goats.

stepByStep.text: There are 10 animals. Suppose all were hens with 2 legs each.
Find the extra legs.
Each goat has 2 more legs than a hen.
Check with 4 goats and 6 hens.
The farmer has 4 goats.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of hens. The question asks for the goats.
misconceptions.B: You got it! 4 goats and 6 hens have 16 + 12 = 28 legs and 10 heads.
misconceptions.C: This divides 28 legs by 4, as if every animal were a goat. There would then be only 7 heads, not 10.
misconceptions.D: This divides 28 legs by 2, as if every animal were a hen. There are only 10 animals in all.

questionText: The digits of a 2-digit number add up to 9. When the two digits swap places, the new number is 27 more than the first number. What is the first number?
hints: List the 2-digit numbers that fit the first clue. Then test each one with the second clue.
Numbers whose digits add up to 9 are 18, 27, and so on. The swapped number is bigger, so the first number has the smaller digit in the tens place. Test each by swapping and subtracting.
A similar problem: the digits add up to 7 and the swapped number is 9 more. Test 16: 61 − 16 = 45. Test 25: 52 − 25 = 27. Test 34: 43 − 34 = 9. So the number is 34.

stepByStep.text: Numbers with digits adding up to 9 and a smaller tens digit are 18, 27, 36 and 45.
Swap the digits of each and subtract.
Only one of them grows by 27 when its digits swap.
The first number is 36.

misconceptions.A: This is the number after the swap. The first number is the smaller one, with the digits the other way round.
misconceptions.B: This is how much bigger the new number is. Testing 27 itself gives 72 − 27 = 45, which is not the right gap.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! 63 − 36 = 27, and 3 + 6 = 9.
misconceptions.D: Swapping gives 54, which is only 9 more than 45. The new number must be 27 more.

questionText: A laddoo is hidden in one of three boxes. Each box has a label. The label on Box 1 says: The laddoo is in this box. The label on Box 2 says: The laddoo is not in this box. The label on Box 3 says: The laddoo is not in Box 1. Only one of the three labels is true. Where is the laddoo?
hints: Suppose the laddoo is in one box, and count how many labels would then be true. Do this for each box in turn.
Suppose the laddoo is in Box 1. Is the label on Box 1 true? Is the label on Box 2 true? Count the true labels and compare with what the question says.

A similar problem: a coin is in one of two tins, and you are told that both labels are untrue. The label on Tin 1 says: The coin is in Tin 2. The label on Tin 2 says: The coin is in this tin. If the coin were in Tin 2, both labels would be true. If it is in Tin 1, both labels are untrue, just as you were told. So the coin is in Tin 1.

stepByStep.text: If the laddoo is in Box 1: the labels on Box 1 and Box 2 are both true. That is two true labels, so this does not fit.
If the laddoo is in Box 3: the labels on Box 2 and Box 3 are both true. That is two true labels again.
If the laddoo is in Box 2: the label on Box 1 is untrue, the label on Box 2 is untrue, and the label on Box 3 is true. Exactly one label is true.
The laddoo is in Box 2.

misconceptions.A: If the laddoo were in Box 1, the labels on Box 1 and Box 2 would both be true. Only one label may be true.
misconceptions.B: If the laddoo were in Box 3, the labels on Box 2 and Box 3 would both be true. Only one label may be true.
misconceptions.C: It can be worked out by testing each box in turn and counting the true labels. Only one box leaves exactly one true label.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! With the laddoo in Box 2, only the label on Box 3 is true.

questionText: A boy has six number cards: 4, 4, 4, 9, 9, 9. He uses 5 of the cards to make a 3-digit number and a 2-digit number. Which of these can be the difference between the 3-digit number and the 2-digit number?
hints: Every digit must be a 4 or a 9. Think about how big or small the two numbers can be, and what the last digit of their difference can be.
Look at the ones place first. 4 − 4 and 9 − 9 give 0, 9 − 4 gives 5, and 14 − 9 gives 5. So the difference must end in 0 or 5. Which choices are still possible?
Similar example: with cards 3, 3, 3, 8, 8, 8, can the difference be 350? Try 388 − 38 = 350. It uses the cards 3, 8, 8, 3, 8, which is two 3s and three 8s, so it can be made.

stepByStep.text: The 3-digit number starts with 4 or 9, so it is between 444 and 499, or between 944 and 999. The 2-digit number is between 44 and 99.
Taking away a number from 44 to 99 leaves a difference from 345 to 455, or from 845 to 955. So 150 and 550 cannot be made.
With only 4s and 9s, the ones digit of the difference is 0 or 5. So 359 cannot be made.
Check the choice that is left. 499 − 49 uses the cards 4, 9, 9, 4, 9, which is two 4s and three 9s.
So the difference can be 450.

misconceptions.A: With only 4s and 9s, the ones digit of the difference is always 0 or 5, so it can never end in 9.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 499 − 49 = 450, and it uses two 4s and three 9s, which the boy has.
misconceptions.C: A 3-digit number starting with 4 gives a difference of at most 455, and one starting with 9 gives at least 845. 550 falls in the gap between.
misconceptions.D: The smallest 3-digit number he can make is 444. Even after taking away 99, the difference is 345, so 150 is too small.
